text: People usually pay money when they need someone to repair a chair or teach
them a new skill. However, residents of the town of Brookfield have another
option. They can join a "time bank," a program in which people exchange help
without using money. Members earn one time credit for every hour they
spend helping someone. They can then use their credits to receive help from
other members. The program aims to bring neighbors together by giving
everyone an opportunity to contribute.
To join, residents complete a form describing the skills they can offer and the
help they need. A coordinator uses this information to connect members. An
hour of gardening earns the same credit as an hour of computer lessons, even
if one of these services usually costs more. Members do not have to help the
person who helped them. For example, someone who repairs a bicycle can
use the credit to get cooking lessons from a different member.
When the program began, fewer people joined than the organizers had
expected. At first, the organizers thought residents were too busy to take
part. However, conversations with local people revealed a different problem:
many believed they had nothing useful to offer. In response, the organizers
held meetings where they gave examples of simple tasks, such as watering
plants while a neighbor was away. More residents joined after they realized
that professional training was not necessary.
One of the new members was sixteen-year-old Adam, who helped an older
resident organize photographs on her phone. Later, he used his credits to
receive help preparing for a job interview from another member, a retired
manager. Adam had originally joined to gain practical experience, but he
discovered an additional benefit. Before joining, he rarely spoke to the adults
on his street. Now, he feels more comfortable asking them for advice, and
several have asked him for help with their phones.
The time bank still faces difficulties. Some requests remain unanswered
because nobody with the right skills is available. In addition, members
sometimes cancel arrangements at the last minute, leaving others without the
help they expected. The organizers are considering a reminder system, but
they have not introduced it yet. Although the program cannot replace every
paid service, they believe it offers something valuable: a chance for people to
recognize abilities in themselves and in their neighbors.
